ca_mammoth_lakes_area.blurb: Mammoth Lakes sits high on the east side of the Sierra, a short drive north of Bishop, and its climbing is spread across a large stretch of country from Rock Creek in the south to the crags north of town. Bouldering is the biggest part of the picture, followed by sport and a solid share of trad, with a few alpine and mixed lines. Sport mostly runs from 5.9 to 5.12, centred on 5.10 and 5.11, while the boulder problems are weighted toward the easier V grades with a tail of hard ones. The rock changes by zone: volcanic tuff gives short, pocketed sport routes at Clark Canyon, while granite offers longer alpine-flavoured lines such as Crystal Crag. Expect a season that opens around late spring and runs into November, with some boulders near the highway usable all year.

wa_icicle_creek.blurb: Icicle Creek runs through a canyon west of Leavenworth on the dry east side of the Cascades, and it is one of the state's busiest climbing zones. Boulders make up nearly half of what is here, with trad and sport crags making up most of the rest and a small amount of ice in the cold months. The rock is coarse-grained granitic stone, in terrain flatter and drier than the west-side valleys. Roped climbing is moderate in feel: lots of 5.7 to 5.11 with a thin top end, and bouldering that covers every grade up to the hard stuff. Crags are scattered, some beside the road and some a long uphill walk in, so there are both crowded spots and quiet ones. Shaded north-facing walls such as Pearly Gates suit summer days, and winter is chilly for rock. Lower Icicle Canyon, Eight Mile and Snow Creek are among the larger sub-areas.

wy_lander_area.blurb: Lander is a small Wyoming town at the foot of the Wind River Range, and it serves as the base for a cluster of mostly sport crags. Sport climbing dominates by a wide margin, with steady numbers of boulder problems and only a sprinkling of trad. Grades lean hard: the bulk of the routes sit between 5.10 and 5.13, with a handful of moderates and some 5.14. Sinks Canyon, at roughly 6,500 feet, can be climbed year-round, with south-facing walls in winter and shade in summer. Wild Iris, around 8,700 feet, is pocketed limestone with short, steep routes and is better outside winter. Baldwin Creek, west of town, offers uniformly steep dolomite aimed at strong climbers. Fossil Hill is another sizable zone.

co_clear_creek_canyon.blurb: Clear Creek Canyon is a narrow gorge just west of Golden, with most of its crags a short walk from highway pullouts. Sport climbing is the main event, backed by a big bouldering collection and a modest amount of trad, plus a little ice and mixed in winter. The rock is a mix of gneiss, schist and sandy granite that is generally solid. Most roped routes fall between 5.9 and 5.13, with the largest share in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, though easier walls exist for beginners, such as High Wire Crag and Little Eiger. The harder lines gather at the New River Wall and nearby formations. Walls face every direction, so climbers can pick sun on cold days or shade on hot ones, which keeps the canyon usable through most of the year.

wv_coopers_rock_state_forest.blurb: Coopers Rock is a state forest on the rim of the Cheat River Gorge, a short drive east of Morgantown, and it is mainly a bouldering destination. Boulders far outnumber the handful of top-rope and trad lines. The stone is a coarse, quartz-rich sandstone that climbers call gritstone, with sloping holds, rounded jugs and shallow pockets. Problems span the full scale, with a large pile of V0 to V5 and a thinner stretch up to around V12. The rock dries slowly after rain: Tilted Tree usually dries first, while Roadside and Upper Rock City take longer. Beyond those, Lower Rock City and the Furnace Road boulders add to a spread-out collection scattered through the woods.

co_canon_city.blurb: Canon City lies in south-central Colorado, and its climbing is built around the Shelf Road cliffs a short drive north of town. Nearly everything here is bolted sport on steep, vertical limestone, spread along several cliff bands with approaches that mostly take under half an hour. The grades centre on 5.10 to 5.12, with plenty of 5.8 and 5.9 for newer leaders and a small number of 5.13s. A few trad lines and boulder problems round out the mix, and Four Mile Creek holds a separate bouldering collection. The town has a mild climate with many sunny days and light snow that melts fast, which makes the area a popular winter, fall and spring stop. Phantom Canyon and Buckskin Crags add smaller options.
